title: Zakat and sadaqah
hook: zakat is required and measured; sadaqah is any gift, any time

segments.voice: Yesterday, giving with dignity, and your line: their right. The poor's share already sits inside the giver's wealth. Did you give anything quietly, and leave it unmentioned? Day one thousand one hundred three.

A smile at the bus stop. A rock kicked off the sidewalk so nobody trips. A bill that comes due once a year, worked out to the decimal. Which of these is charity? According to a set of sayings of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, all of them can be. But only one of them is zakat. Two of Islam's words for giving sit side by side like two hands. One is measured, owed, and dated. The other has no amount, no season, and no minimum. Today, the difference between them, and how the two fit together.
screen: `A SMILE. A ROCK. A YEARLY BILL.` → `ALL CHARITY?` → `TWO WORDS FOR GIVING.`

segments.voice: First, zakat. These past days have walked through it: a pillar, owed by those whose wealth passes the threshold, measured by a rate, due on a yearly date, sent to the eight groups the Qur'an names. Required, and counted. Second, sadaqah. Sadaqah has no fixed amount and no fixed day. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet ﷺ says that every good deed is sadaqah. Other reports fill in the list: removing something harmful from the road, a good word, and in a report in at-Tirmidhi, smiling in your brother's face. Third, the two overlap, and the language shows it. The verse that names the eight groups who receive zakat, surah nine, verse sixty, actually uses the word sadaqat, the plural of sadaqah. Pickthall translates it simply: "The alms are only for the poor and the needy." That verse is read as the list for zakat. So the line between the words is not a wall. Zakat is a kind of sadaqah that has been made obligatory and given a measure. Fourth, what happens when someone has nothing to give. Another report in Bukhari takes that question head on. Every Muslim owes sadaqah, the Prophet ﷺ says. The companions ask: and if a person has nothing? Then work with your hands, benefit yourself, and give. And if they can't? Help someone in need. And if they can't do that? Do good and hold back from harm; that counts as sadaqah too. So a single day can hold two kinds of giving. One is a duty with a calculator. The other is open all day, and costs as little as a kind face.
screen: `ZAKAT: OWED, MEASURED, DATED.` · `SADAQAH: ANY GOOD DEED.` · `9:60 SAYS SADAQAT.` · `NOTHING TO GIVE? STILL A WAY.` · then, large: `THE ALMS ARE ONLY FOR THE POOR AND THE NEEDY.`

segments.voice: The practice: give sadaqah today, and choose it now. Sit back, and let your breath slow. Walk through the hours ahead of you in your mind: where you'll be, who you'll pass, who will message you. Find one place where a small gift fits. It might be a few coins or a few dollars. It might be a sincere word to someone who works hard and hears little thanks. It might be clearing something out of a path. Pick one, and see yourself doing it. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it. The bell holds the time.
Zakat and sadaqah. Zakat: the required share, measured and yearly. Sadaqah: any good given freely, at any time, in any amount. Today's word.
Your line: required and freely. Today, do the one small sadaqah you chose, and notice that nobody asked you to. Day one thousand one hundred three.

howItsDone: Muslims pay zakat once a year on qualifying wealth, and give sadaqah whenever they choose, in money, food, help or kind words.

original.note: Arabic: voluntary charity, any good given freely, in any amount, at any time.

trapdoor: what you thought: zakat and sadaqah are two names for the same thing.
what it means: zakat is the required, measured share; sadaqah is any good given freely.
what a scholar hears: 9:60 calls zakat as-sadaqat; zakat is sadaqah made obligatory and measured.
